message.content:
**Answer**

The last common ancestor of a lion (*Panthera leo*) and a zebra (*Equus quagga*) is a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived roughly 70–80 million years ago, during the late Cretaceous/early Paleogene. This ancestor was part of the clade **Laurasiatheria**, which gave rise to many modern mammalian orders, including:

| Order | Modern representatives | Approximate divergence from Laurasiatheria |
|-------|------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| **Carnivora** (lion’s lineage) | Cats, dogs, bears, seals, etc. | ~70 Myr ago |
| **Perissodactyla** (zebra’s lineage) | Horses, rhinos, tapirs | ~70 Myr ago |

So, the common ancestor of lions and zebras is the last common ancestor of the orders **Carnivora** and **Perissodactyla**—a small, likely insect‑eating mammal that lived about 70–80 million years ago. This ancestor is far older than the last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria), but it is the most recent point at which the evolutionary lineages of lions and zebras shared a single organism.
message.reasoning: The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage. Both are mammals, but lions are felids (family Felidae), zebras are equids (family Equidae). They diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla. Actually, lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla. So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps a placental mammal ancestor. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the eutherian ancestor. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: that would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both orders, which is the clade of Laurasiatheria? Actually, Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of the clade Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria. That ancestor would be a small mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago. So the answer: the last common ancestor of lions and zebras is a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived in the late Cretaceous or early Paleogene, part of Laurasiatheria. Alternatively, the last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria). But the question likely expects "the last common ancestor of the two species is a small mammal that lived about 70 million years ago, belonging to the Laurasiatheria clade." Or "the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago." So answer accordingly.
